lesson.title: One World, One Standard: Inside the International Organization for Standardization
lesson.summary: ISO is a federation of national standards bodies that produces formal international standards across nearly every industry, and in networking is best known for publishing the OSI reference model that many students still use to reason about protocol layers.
lesson.body:
The International Organization for Standardization, almost always called ISO, is a federation of national standards bodies, one per member country, such as ANSI representing the United States, that together produce voluntary international standards spanning nearly every industry imaginable, from screw threads to food safety to computer networking. It is headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland, and unlike the open, individual-participation model of the IETF from the previous chapter, ISO standards are typically developed through technical committees where each participating country sends official delegates, and a standard is only adopted once member bodies formally vote to approve it.

Even the organization's short name has a deliberate story behind it, and it is a fact ISO itself confirms: "ISO" is not actually an acronym. The full name translates differently in each language, for instance "International Organization for Standardization" in English versus "Organisation internationale de normalisation" in French, which would produce different abbreviations in different countries. Instead, the founders chose "ISO" from the Greek word isos, meaning equal, so the short name would be identical no matter what language it appeared in, which is a fittingly literal example of what standardization itself is trying to achieve.

ISO's most influential contribution to networking is the Open Systems Interconnection reference model, published jointly with the international body now known as the ITU-T as ISO/IEC 7498 during the early 1980s. The OSI model describes networking as seven stacked layers, physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation, and application, each responsible for one part of the overall communication problem and each depending only on the layer directly below it. It remains one of the most widely taught frameworks for reasoning about where a given protocol fits, which is why you will often hear TCP described as a transport-layer protocol or Ethernet described as a data-link-layer protocol even though neither was designed as part of the OSI protocol suite itself. That is an important nuance: the OSI reference model as a conceptual map became hugely influential, but the actual OSI protocols ISO defined to go with it were largely never adopted, and the TCP/IP protocol suite developed through the IETF became the internet's real foundation instead.

ISO fits into the pattern the earlier Standard chapter introduced, as a formal, de jure standards body with versioned, official documents, but its governance style sits at the opposite end of the spectrum from the IETF's open mailing lists. ISO standards documents also traditionally must be purchased rather than downloaded for free the way RFCs are, another reminder that different standards bodies, even when they are all producing legitimate, authoritative documents, operate under genuinely different rules about participation and access.

Beyond networking, ISO standards touch daily life constantly, from ISO 8601, which defines the YYYY-MM-DD date format used throughout computing, to ISO 9001, a widely adopted quality management framework used across manufacturing and services. Seeing the same organization behind both a date format buried in a network protocol and a factory's quality certification is a useful reminder of just how broad the idea of a standard really is, extending far past the networking-specific bodies covered in the surrounding chapters.
